items.title: 11.1.2 Domains and Ranges of Secant Function

blocks.alt: Unit circle with centre O at the origin, axes X prime X and Y prime Y. It meets the axes at A(1, 0), B(0, 1), C(minus 1, 0) and D(0, minus 1). The terminal side OP, drawn as an arrow, makes angle theta with OX; P(x, y) is on the circle, M is the foot of the perpendicular PM on OX, OM = x and MP = y.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.1 (repeated from 11.1): unit circle with P(x, y) on the terminal side of θ (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
\[\sec\theta = \frac{1}{x},\quad x \ne 0\]
\(\Rightarrow\) terminal side \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) should not coincide with \(OY\) or \(OY'\) (the \(Y\)-axis)
\[\Rightarrow \theta \ne \pm\frac{\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{5\pi}{2}, \ldots\]
\[\Rightarrow \theta \ne (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2},\ \text{where } n \in \mathbb{Z}\]
Domain of secant function \(= \mathbb{R} - \{x \mid x = (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2},\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: As in 11.1.1, the line of excluded angles is printed jumbled in the book (\(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{5\pi}{2}\) overlap). It should read \(\theta \ne \pm\frac{\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{5\pi}{2}, \ldots\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Secant has the same denominator as tangent: \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}\) and \(\tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\). Both fail exactly when \(x = \cos\theta = 0\), i.e. on the \(Y\)-axis. So secant and tangent have the same domain.

As \(0 \le x \le 1\) so, \(\frac{1}{x} \ge 1\), \(\sec\theta \ge 1\) and \(-1 \le x \le 0\) so, \(\frac{1}{x} \le -1\), \(\sec\theta \le -1\)
As \(\sec\theta\) attains all real values except those between \(-1\) and \(1\),
Range of secant function \(= \mathbb{R} - \{x \mid -1 < x < 1\}\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book writes \(0 \le x \le 1\) and \(-1 \le x \le 0\), but \(x = 0\) is not allowed (\(\frac{1}{0}\) has no value; we have just excluded it). The correct statements are:
\[0 < x \le 1 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{x} \ge 1\]
\[-1 \le x < 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{x} \le -1\]
The conclusion (the range) is not affected.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does taking the reciprocal push the value outside \((-1, 1)\)? Dividing \(1\) by a positive number that is at most \(1\) gives at least \(1\): \(\frac{1}{1} = 1\), \(\frac{1}{0.5} = 2\), \(\frac{1}{0.1} = 10\). The smaller the positive \(x\), the larger \(\frac{1}{x}\). For negative \(x\) the same happens with a minus sign: \(\frac{1}{-0.25} = -4\).
So \(\sec\theta\) can never be, for example, \(\frac{1}{2}\): that would need \(\cos\theta = 2\), which is outside the range of cosine.
In interval notation the range is \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\). The values \(1\) and \(-1\) are included: \(\sec 0 = 1\) and \(\sec\pi = -1\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Remember the shape of the answer: \(|\sec\theta| \ge 1\) for every \(\theta\) in the domain. Any question such as "Is \(\sec\theta = 0.7\) possible?" has the answer no.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{x}\) needs \(x \ne 0\): domain \(\mathbb{R} - \{(2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2} : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\), the same as tangent.
2. Range: \(\mathbb{R} - (-1, 1) = (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\), i.e. \(\sec\theta \le -1\) or \(\sec\theta \ge 1\).
3. \(\sec\theta = 1\) at \(\theta = 0\) and \(\sec\theta = -1\) at \(\theta = \pi\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing the range of secant as \([-1, 1]\): that is the range of cosine. Secant is its reciprocal, so it lies outside that interval.
2. Excluding \(-1\) and \(1\) from the range. Only the numbers strictly between them are missing.
3. Allowing \(x = 0\) in the working: never write \(\frac{1}{0}\).
